title: A Geometric Theory of Fermion-to-Qubit Encodings
authors: Lakshya Nagpal, Nishith Reen, S. R. Hassan
abstract: Exact fermion to qubit transformations are conventionally regarded as algorithmic tools that translate many-body Hamiltonians into qubit representations for quantum simulation. Here we show that they also define intrinsic geometric representations whose structure encodes physically meaningful information beyond spectral equivalence. We develop a geometric framework based on weighted hypergraphs and coupling space representations constructed from the Bravyi--Kitaev (BK) and Xia--Bian--Kais (XBK) encodings. Within the BK representation, we introduce a geometric observable that compares the algebraic connectivities of the kinetic and interaction hypergraphs, derive its exact analytical dependence on interaction strength, and uncover two geometric universality classes together with an exact spectral organization originating from the binary tree architecture of the encoding. The complementary XBK representation describes the evolution of encoded Hamiltonians through probability measures in coupling space, where optimal transport quantifies interaction-driven reorganization independently of the spectral analysis. Applications to the Hubbard, spinless tV , single impurity Anderson, and Kitaev models demonstrate that these connectivity and transport based geometric descriptions consistently capture the structural evolution of encoded quantum Hamiltonians across distinct classes of many-body systems. Our results establish hypergraph geometry as a new framework for understanding fermion-to-qubit encodings,revealing that they serve not only as computational mappings but also as geometric representations of quantum many-body Hamiltonians.
summary: This work introduces a geometric framework using weighted hypergraphs to analyze fermion-to-qubit mappings. It shows that these encodings encode more than just spectral information by defining measurable geometric structures. By comparing connectivity metrics (BK) and transport measures (XBK), the authors provide a universal tool to track structural changes in complex quantum Hamiltonians like the Hubbard model.
main_problem: To determine if fermion-to-qubit encodings reveal physical structure beyond merely reproducing the spectrum of the original many-body Hamiltonian.
main_result: The framework establishes hypergraph geometry as a general tool, showing that connectivity and transport metrics consistently capture the structural evolution of encoded Hamiltonians across diverse correlated systems.
method: Developing a geometric framework using weighted hypergraphs to analyze two complementary views: spectral connectivity (via graph Laplacians in BK encoding) and coupling-space reorganization (via optimal transport in XBK encoding).
model_or_system: The analysis applies to general interacting fermionic Hamiltonians, exemplified by the Hubbard model, spinless tV chain, single-impurity Anderson model, and Kitaev chain.
key_observables: Geometric observables like $ho(U) = \lambda_2(L_{hop})/\lambda_2(L_{int})$ (BK) and Wasserstein distance $W(\mu_1, \mu_2)$ (XBK).
important_parameters: Interaction strength ($U$), hopping parameters ($t$), and the characteristic crossover scale $U^*$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping the hypergraph to an equivalent weighted graph using standard clique expansion, and that geometric observables capture physical reorganization.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structural evolution across multiple correlated models, showing consistent signatures of interaction-driven reorganization via spectral observables (BK) and distance comparisons.
paper_structure: The paper develops a general hypergraph geometry framework, applies it to specific encodings (BK and XBK), derives key geometric observables that quantify connectivity changes, and demonstrates the consistency of these findings across several canonical strongly correlated models.
why_interesting: It provides powerful, non-spectral diagnostic tools (hypergraph geometry) to analyze how quantum information encoding schemes map physical interactions into structural constraints, which is highly relevant for understanding complex many-body physics simulations.

(b) Representative distributions of U ∗ k illustrating the persistence of the two spectral families. (c) Number of tree-dominated modes as a function of the number of qubits. Every system satisfies the exact relation Ntree = nq/4, demonstrating that the interaction spectrum possesses a universal internal organization determined solely by the geometry of the Bravyi–Kitaev encoding.

FIG. 4: Interaction-driven reweighting of the encoded hypergraph. Rows correspond to different Hubbard clusters, while columns show increasing interaction strengths. Blue edges represent hopping-derived Pauli interactions and red edges represent interaction-derived Pauli interactions. Node colour denotes the local metallic character ξ, while node size is proportional to the weighted degree. Increasing interaction strength produces a continuous redistribution of coupling weight from kinetic to interaction sectors without changing the underlying connectivity of the network.
